newsitem.title: USA: Senate leader Lott says "too late" for CPI budget fix.
newsitem.headline: Senate leader Lott says "too late" for CPI budget fix.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said Monday it was "too late" to include a consumer price index adjustment in budget negotiations with the White House, dealing a blow to a major deficit-cutting idea.

The Mississippi Republican's comment came one day after President Clinton signalled flexibility on that item, which has been mentioned since the start of this year as a way to help reach the goal of balancing the budget by 2002.
"The CPI ... I think that's by the boards now, it's too late," Lott told reporters.
The inflation measure entered the budget realm this year after an advisory commission in December said it overstated cost of living by about 1.1 percentage points per year.

The issue is politically sensitive because reducing the cost of living increase would affect federal benefit programmes such as Social Security for the elderly. Increases in those benefits are tied to the price index.

However, it would mean savings in federal spending and make reducing the budget deficit easier. Neither party has been anxious to take the first step on the price index for fear of being accused by the other of cutting back benefits to the elderly.

Lott earlier this year called for a blue-ribbon commission to look at the index and recommend a solution. Clinton balked at the idea. But Sunday, Clinton appeared to offer an olive branch to the Republican leader by saying in a television interview that he was willing to "take some heat" on a cost of living adjustment.
Now it is Lott who is saying the idea will not fly, citing lack of support among House Republicans and Democrats and essentially rendering the issue dead for this year.
"It's going to be awfully hard for us to ask our people in the Senate to walk the plank" on an issue that would spark opposition from elderly and labour groups, Lott said.
"Time was of the essence, and the time has come and gone," he added.
Lott said he hoped to speak to Clinton Tuesday, but added that the president needed to cut back on domestic spending increases he was seeking.
Lott said the White House was talking about $120 billion to $130 billion in new spending over five years for non-defence domestic programmes and entitlements.
The Lott comments came as the White House and Congress stepped up their drive to reach a balanced budget agreement that would give each side some of what it wanted.
The Senate leader said Monday evening that he was "hopeful" an agreement would be reached this week after speaking with key budget negotiators.

Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, and House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich, an Ohio Republican, were both fairly "upbeat" about the status of budget talks, Lott said.
"They still feel like they might get something done here in the next couple of days and so ... I'm hopeful," he said.
Budget discussions were expected to go on Monday night and Tuesday morning, Lott said.
If a budget agreement is not reached with the White House, Republicans will look toward formulating their own budget.

Even if a budget pact was reached between congressional leaders and the White House, there would be no guarantee it would pass Congress, where members of both parties warned they could reject a deal that did not contain their priorities.
Some Republicans are adamant about wanting larger tax cuts than Democrats, and some Democrats do not want to cut back on spending for domestic programmes as much as Republicans.
